sector: Real Estate - Retail REIT (Flagship City-Centre Destinations)
overview: Hammerson is a UK-listed REIT that invests in, develops and manages a concentrated portfolio of prime, retail-led 'flagship' city-centre destinations in the UK, Ireland and France, including Bullring & Grand Central (Birmingham), Cabot Circus (Bristol), Highcross (Leicester), The Oracle (Reading), Westquay (Southampton), Union Square (Aberdeen), Manchester Arndale (50%, acquired July 2026), Dundrum Town Centre and The Ilac Centre (Dublin), and Les Terrasses du Port and Les 3 Fontaines (France). Having spent 2019-2024 repairing a balance sheet badly overstretched going into the pandemic (via a 2020 rights issue, the sale of its VIA Outlets stake, and the 2024 full exit of its Value Retail/Bicester Village stake), the group is now in an acquisitive growth phase, buying out joint-venture partners in its own flagship assets (Bullring, Brent Cross, The Oracle) and adding new scale (Manchester Arndale) funded by equity placings, recycled disposal proceeds and bond issuance, while operating an 'integrated pure-play' in-house asset management and leasing platform across all three countries.

business_model.summary: Hammerson earns rental income from long-leasehold ownership and active management of a small number of very large, prime 'flagship' shopping/leisure destinations, supplemented by service charge recovery, car parking, specialty/short-term leasing, brand partnerships (events, marketing, media) and development/repositioning gains. The strategy has shifted decisively from being a diversified multi-asset UK shopping centre landlord (pre-2020) to a concentrated owner-operator of ~10-11 'best in class' flagship destinations, now wholly or near-wholly owned (following a multi-year programme of buying out joint-venture partners) rather than held through 50/50 JVs, which the company argues gives it full operating control and clean reported numbers. Growth comes from a combination of like-for-like net rental income growth (driven by leasing at positive reversion to ERV, rising occupancy and footfall), accretive acquisitions (Manchester Arndale, buyouts of JV stakes), and 'strategic land' optionality (repositioning old department-store space and adjacent land into residential, PBSA student housing, leisure or mixed-use schemes).

revenue_streams.name: Net rental income (flagship UK destinations)
revenue_streams.description: Core rental income from the 10 UK/Ireland flagships (Bullring & Grand Central, Cabot Circus, Highcross, The Oracle, Westquay, Union Square, Manchester Arndale, Dundrum, The Ilac Centre); H1 2026 group NRI was £112m (+40% YoY), driven by JV buyouts and the Arndale acquisition plus 5% like-for-like growth

revenue_streams.name: France flagship destinations (Les Terrasses du Port, Les 3 Fontaines)
revenue_streams.description: Marseille and Cergy destinations; occupancy ~90-99%, Les 3 Fontaines ended FY25 at 90% occupancy (highest since pre-COVID) with the pre-let Cergy 3/Primark-Nike redevelopment adding income in late 2026

revenue_streams.name: Strategic land / development & repositioning
revenue_streams.description: £291m of remaining strategic land book value (pro forma) spanning integral/adjacent residential and mixed-use schemes (Edgbaston Gardens, The Drum at Grand Central, Cabot Gate PBSA, Martineau Galleries) and standalone opportunities (The Goodsyard, The Oracle); The Ironworks residential scheme at Dundrum (122 units) launched October 2025, 80% leased by FY25

revenue_streams.name: Specialty leasing, commercialisation and brand partnerships
revenue_streams.description: Short-term/temporary lettings, brand promotions (~500 in FY25), events, media and partnership deals (Tesla, Sephora, Aston Villa, Diet Coke) that drive incremental income and footfall without long leases

business_model.customer_type: B2B (national and international retail, leisure and F&B occupiers/brands as tenants) with the ultimate end customer being B2C shoppers/visitors; no direct consumer-facing retail business of its own
business_model.geographic_mix: UK/Ireland flagships (~10 of the destinations, the large majority of portfolio value) plus France (Les Terrasses du Port, Les 3 Fontaines); portfolio valued at £4.4bn (AUM) / £3.5-3.6bn attributable portfolio value as of H1 2026, with 98% of value rated 'A' by Green Street
business_model.unit_economics: Flagship occupancy 96% at FY2025 (up from 95%), rising to 95.6% group / highest H1 occupancy in seven years by H1 2026; FY25 record leasing of £51m on 1.6m sq ft at +18% like-for-like vs ERV on a net effective basis (fourth consecutive year of double-digit positive leasing spreads); average net initial yield ~7.6-7.8% on recent acquisitions (Manchester Arndale topped-up NIY 7.8%, Bullring/Grand Central buyout at 7.7%).

main_competitors: Local/regional shopping centre owners and private equity real estate funds
Online retail/e-commerce as a demand-side substitute for physical footfall
competitive_position.market_position: One of the UK's leading owners of large-format, prime 'super-regional' and city-centre flagship shopping/leisure destinations, concentrated in a small number (~10-11) of the UK and Ireland's top-performing retail venues (all ranked in the top 20 retail venues across their geographies, and the top 1% by catchment retail spend), plus two French flagships; smaller and more narrowly focused than diversified mixed-use peers Landsec and British Land, and smaller in scale than pan-European giant Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield, but differentiated by its 'pure-play' retail-destination specialism and in-house integrated operating platform.
competitive_position.market_share: Niche/concentrated rather than broad — owns a small number of the largest and highest-footfall retail destinations in its core markets (e.g., Bullring is one of the UK's top-performing retail-anchored destinations; Manchester Arndale has the largest catchment outside London at 6.4m), rather than competing on volume/breadth of a large diversified portfolio

moat_factors.description: Core destinations are large, well-located, city-centre or super-regional schemes with very high barriers to new supply (new large-format retail development is now rare in the UK), giving pricing power in a 'flight to quality'/polarisation environment where occupiers are consolidating into fewer, larger, better stores

In-house asset management, leasing, data/analytics and placemaking capability across all destinations (increasingly via full ownership rather than JVs), which management argues drives superior leasing outcomes (record £51m leasing value in FY25, +18% LfL vs ERV) and cost efficiency (EPRA cost ratio cut from 38.3% to 28.4% YoY by H1 2026)

98% of portfolio value rated 'A' by Green Street; destinations serve catchments of c.500,000+ population within 30 minutes and >40% under-35 demographics, aligning with the 'cities are engines of growth' and 'polarisation' themes management cites as structural tailwinds

Fitch upgraded to A- and Moody's outlook moved to positive (Baa2) in October 2025; this access to debt/bond and equity capital markets (two oversubscribed bond issues, two oversubscribed equity placings in 2025-26) is a moat versus smaller, less creditworthy private landlords competing for the same prime assets

Long-term relationships with major brands (M&S, Zara, Sephora, Uniqlo, Primark) and a track record of winning 'portfolio firsts' (35+ brands joining or expanding into the portfolio in FY25) support occupancy and rental tension, though occupier bargaining power remains significant given alternatives (other prime destinations, online, out-of-town retail parks)

weaknesses: Small scale and high geographic/asset concentration — a handful of flagship destinations dominate NAV and earnings, so a problem at any single large asset (anchor failure, major redevelopment delay, local economic shock) has an outsized impact

Heavily UK-weighted and therefore exposed to UK consumer, planning and political/regulatory conditions (business rates, UK retail sector structural decline narrative) more than globally diversified peers like URW

Balance sheet still carries elevated leverage on an annualised basis (net debt:EBITDA 8.1x at H1 2026, down from 9.5x at FY2025 year-end but well above the company's own 6-8x 'guiderail') following debt-funded JV buyouts and acquisitions, re-introducing some of the leverage sensitivity the 2020 rights issue was designed to remove

No remaining exposure to the structurally faster-growing European outlet/outlet-village retail format — Hammerson fully exited Value Retail (Bicester Village owner) in September 2024 for ~£600m and VIA Outlets in 2020, so unlike some diversified peers it has no outlet-sector diversification left

Dependent on continued occupier demand for large-format physical retail; a reversal of the current 'flight to quality/polarisation' trend (e.g., renewed e-commerce share gains, consumer downturn) would disproportionately hit a pure-play physical retail landlord with no logistics/industrial or office diversification

growth_drivers: Portfolio repositioning and active asset management: record FY2025 leasing (£51m on 1.6m sq ft, +18% LfL vs ERV, 4th consecutive year of double-digit positive leasing spreads) continuing into H1 2026 (+17% LfL vs previous passing, +9% vs ERV, pipeline >£20m)

Accretive, scale-building acquisitions: 50% of Manchester Arndale acquired for £218m (topped-up NIY 7.8%, >2% EPS accretive) in July 2026, funded via a ~10% equity placing (~£189-190m net proceeds, 355p/share) — management's stated intent to 'further increase scale' through similar disciplined, selective acquisitions in core UK/Ireland/France markets

Buy-outs of joint-venture partner stakes converting minority-owned assets into full ownership: £618m deployed in FY2025 to acquire JV partners' stakes in Brent Cross, The Oracle and the remaining 50% of Bullring & Grand Central (August 2025, £319m), simplifying the portfolio, removing JV governance friction, and capturing 100% of the upside/control

Strategic land and repositioning pipeline: £291m book value of strategic land with multiple near-term catalysts — The Drum (Grand Central, office-led mixed-use, GDV ~£100m), Martineau Galleries, Cabot Gate (600-bed PBSA, planning secured), Edgbaston Gardens residential, The Ironworks residential at Dundrum (122 units, 80%+ leased)

Continued disposal/capital recycling of non-core assets at premiums to book value (£75m of non-core disposals YTD H1 2026 — Leeds Eastgate, Dublin Central, Zweibrücken), funding reinvestment into higher-quality/higher-growth core assets without over-levering the balance sheet

Structural 'polarisation' tailwind: management and industry data continue to show footfall and sales outperformance concentrating in the best prime destinations (national benchmarks negative or flat while Hammerson's flagships grew footfall/sales ahead of the market in every region in H1 2026), meaning a smaller pool of 'winner' assets — which Hammerson largely owns — should keep capturing disproportionate occupier demand and rental growth

New medium-term guidance (July 2026): 6-8% EPRA EPS CAGR, 6-8% DPS CAGR and c.10% total accounting return off the FY2025 base, implying continued compounding growth in earnings, dividends and NTA rather than a one-off repair/recovery story
Credit rating improvement trajectory (Fitch A-, Moody's Baa2 positive outlook, October 2025) lowering the cost of capital and supporting further oversubscribed bond/equity issuance to fund growth

business.description: Failure to anticipate structural shifts in physical retail (continued e-commerce penetration, occupier consolidation into fewer/larger stores) could impair leasing performance, occupier mix and footfall/spend; company-assessed residual risk is 'Medium', citing flagship destinations, diversified occupier base and 4.3-year average lease term to first break as mitigants

A small number of large flagship destinations drive the majority of value and income; unplanned vacancy, anchor-tenant failure, major redevelopment delay or a localized demand shock at any single large asset would have an outsized group-level impact

Repositioning/development schemes (The Drum, Cabot Gate PBSA, Martineau Galleries, Ironworks residential, Cergy 3) carry complexity, multi-phase execution and exposure to volatile materials/labour/sub-contractor costs; unsuccessful projects could produce adverse financial and reputational outcomes
Failure to retain or recruit key management and specialist asset management/leasing talent could impair execution of the increasingly complex, acquisition-led strategy

business.risk: IT, cyber security and technology (new principal risk in FY2025)
business.description: Newly elevated to its own principal risk category reflecting high-profile UK/global cyber attacks and AI-driven threat escalation; mitigated via ISO 27001-aligned framework, 24/7 managed security service provider and a virtual CISO

financial.description: Net debt £1.4bn at H1 2026 (39% LTV, annualised net debt:EBITDA 8.1x, reducing to a pro forma c.7x after the Dublin Central disposal, Arndale acquisition and associated placing) — materially above the company's own 6-8x 'through the cycle' guiderail following a run of debt- and equity-funded acquisitions; refinancing of £463m/£150m of RCFs (extended to April 2029) and upcoming bond maturities remains a recurring requirement

Weighted average debt maturity 4.8 years but with £104m due 2026, £609m due 2027 and £463m of RCFs maturing April 2027 (since extended to 2029); the FY2025 Viability Statement explicitly flags that 'significant refinancing is required' over the viability period, though the Directors express confidence given demonstrated market access (two oversubscribed bond issues and two oversubscribed equity placings in 2025-26)

Net finance costs guided at c.£60m for FY2026; interest cover covenant headroom assessed to a 75% reduction in net rental income in the FY2025 viability stress test (62% in the stress scenario), indicating moderate but not tight headroom

Property valuations (and hence NTA, gearing and LTV covenants) are exposed to UK/Irish/French commercial real estate yield movements; gearing covenant headroom assessed to a 33% fall in valuations (28% in the viability stress scenario)

Recent growth (Bullring/Grand Central buyout, Manchester Arndale) has been partly funded by repeated equity placings (£135m in August 2025, ~£190m in July/August 2026, each ~10% of shares), diluting existing shareholders even when framed as earnings-accretive per share

regulatory.description: Multi-jurisdiction exposure (UK, Ireland, France) to evolving building safety, employment, planning, economic/financial crime, tax and corporate governance regulation; potential for administrative/cost burden and diversion of management resources, though no material risk increase identified in FY2025

regulatory.risk: UK planning and business rates policy
regulatory.description: UK planning reform and potential changes to business rates/rent regulation are specifically monitored as areas of proposed government change that could affect occupiers and, indirectly, Hammerson's income

Tightening Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards (MEES) requiring 100% of UK units rated EPC C or above by April 2027, and evolving UK Sustainability Reporting Standards, require continued capital investment (NZAP budget £18m for 2026) and disclosure effort, though the EU's 2025 CSRD Omnibus decision has reduced the immediate regulatory burden

macro.risk: Macroeconomic and geopolitical (the Group's sole 'High' residual risk)
macro.description: Persistent inflation, 'higher for longer' UK interest rates, limited GDP growth, supply chain constraints, geopolitical tensions/tariffs/trade wars; explicitly rated High residual risk (increased likelihood but reduced impact per the FY2025 review) given it is 'largely beyond management's control'

Occupier sales and footfall are ultimately a function of UK/Irish/French consumer discretionary spending power; while Hammerson's flagships have recently outperformed national benchmarks, a broader consumer downturn would still pressure occupier trading, rents and valuations

Reduced investor demand for retail real estate (from higher borrowing costs, economic downturn or weaker occupier/customer confidence) could hinder portfolio liquidity, funding availability for reinvestment/refinancing, and capital-recycling execution at attractive pricing

Physical climate risks (extreme weather, flooding) and transition risks assessed across all core assets via CRREM and Marsh-led TCFD-aligned modelling; 90% of portfolio currently assessed in line with a Paris-aligned 1.5°C decarbonisation pathway

macro_factors.industry_outlook: UK, Irish and French physical retail property is bifurcating sharply: national footfall and sales benchmarks have been flat-to-negative in several recent periods, but prime, large-format, well-located 'flagship' destinations (Hammerson's core focus) are seeing a genuine flight-to-quality as occupiers consolidate into fewer, larger, better stores, driving record positive leasing spreads and rising occupancy at the top end even as secondary retail property remains structurally challenged. Scarcity of new prime supply (minimal new large-format retail development in the UK) supports pricing power for owners of irreplaceable assets.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate-to-high — rental income and occupancy are relatively sticky in the near term (long leases, high occupancy), but footfall, sales, leasing demand, capital values and investor appetite for retail real estate are all sensitive to the broader economic/consumer cycle and to UK/Irish/French interest-rate and inflation conditions.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High — REIT model is capital-intensive and debt-funded (net debt £1.4bn, LTV 39%); financing costs, refinancing terms, and property valuations (which drive NTA, gearing and interest-cover covenants) are all directly sensitive to interest rate levels; UK rates are forecast to fall only slowly, which management flags as a modest support for investment-market sentiment.
macro_factors.currency_exposure: Moderate — GBP reporting currency with meaningful Euro-denominated income and debt from the France business and Euro-denominated bonds (e.g., €350m 3.875% bond issued June 2026, €350m 3.5% bond issued October 2025); currency/FX movements flow through the NTA-per-share bridge.
key_input_costs: Cost of debt / credit spreads (bond and RCF financing)
Construction/development materials and labour costs for repositioning and development schemes
Energy costs (partially hedged via a Corporate Purchase Power Agreement covering ~75% of new green electricity for UK destinations)
Service charge costs recovered from occupiers (subject to negotiation/dispute risk)
macro_factors.regulatory_environment: UK planning reform, potential business rates changes, tightening Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards (100% UK units EPC C+ required by April 2027), and evolving UK Sustainability Reporting Standards are the most relevant near-term regulatory themes; EU CSRD burden was reduced by the 2025 Omnibus decision. No major pending legislation specifically threatens the retail-REIT structure itself (REIT tax regime unchanged).

recent_developments.event: Completed the acquisition of a 50% interest in Manchester Arndale (c.2m sq ft, 230+ occupiers, 96% let, 6.4m catchment — the largest outside London, Green Street 'A' rated) for £218m, a topped-up net initial yield of 7.8% and >2% pro-forma EPS accretion for ~1% NTA dilution; funded via a ~10% primary placing plus a RetailBook retail offer and director subscriptions, raising gross proceeds of ~£190m (net ~£189m) at 355p per share, taking total issued shares to 585,217,753.

H1 2026 results: net rental income £112m (+40% YoY), EPRA earnings £64m (+33% YoY), EPRA EPS 12.1p (+22%), interim DPS 9.67p (+22%), EPRA cost ratio cut to 28.4% from 38.3%, portfolio value £3,596m (+1% vs FY25), EPRA NTA per share £3.94 (unchanged YoY), net debt £1.4bn, LTV 39% (pro forma ~36% post Dublin Central disposal/Arndale/placing), annualised net debt:EBITDA 8.1x (pro forma ~7x). Non-core disposals of £75m YTD (Leeds Eastgate, Dublin Central, Zweibrücken) completed at a premium to book value.

Raised FY2026 guidance: EPRA earnings growth of c.27% to c.£132m (c.£125m underlying + £7m from Arndale, up from prior c.£120m underlying guidance), total NRI growth c.28%, like-for-like NRI growth c.4-5%, EPRA cost ratio to fall 300-400bps in FY26 and FY27 (below 30% for FY26), net finance costs c.£60m. Introduced new medium-term guidance off the FY2025 base: 6-8% EPRA EPS CAGR, 6-8% DPS CAGR, c.10% total accounting return.
Issued a €350m 3.875% bond maturing 2031 as part of ongoing refinancing/liability management, alongside extending £463m and £150m RCFs to April 2029.

Credit rating improvements: Fitch upgraded Hammerson's senior unsecured rating to A-; Moody's changed the outlook on its Baa2 long-term debt rating to positive — both cited as reflecting the strengthened balance sheet and growth execution.

Completed the acquisition of the remaining 50% of Bullring & Grand Central (Birmingham) for £319m (4% discount to June 2025 book value, 7.7% topped-up net initial yield), funded via existing cash and a ~10% equity placing (£135m net proceeds at a 2.5% discount to undisturbed price), taking full ownership of one of the UK's top-performing retail destinations.

FY2025: net rental income £180m (+23% YoY), EPRA earnings £104m (+5% YoY), EPRA EPS 20.7p (+4%), full-year DPS 16.50p (+6%), EPRA NTA per share £3.94 (+6%), net assets +£274m (+15%), net debt £1,370m (+£571m YoY) reflecting £618m deployed on JV-partner buyouts (Brent Cross, The Oracle, Bullring/Grand Central stakes), LTV 39% (FY24: 30%), net debt:EBITDA 9.5x reported / 8.1x annualised (FY24: 5.8x). Flagship occupancy rose to 96% (from 95%); record leasing of £51m on 1.6m sq ft at +18% LfL vs ERV.

Completed the full disposal of its remaining ~40% minority stake in Value Retail (owner of Bicester Village and other European luxury outlet villages) to L Catterton (LVMH-backed) affiliates, realising ~£600m of cash at a £1.5bn enterprise valuation for Value Retail; proceeds earmarked for debt reduction, reinvestment in core city-destination assets, and up to £140m of share buybacks — completing Hammerson's exit from the outlet-village format entirely (following the 2020 VIA Outlets disposal).

items.notes: Reflects the Manchester Arndale acquisition and prior-year JV buyouts (Bullring/Grand Central, Brent Cross, The Oracle) annualising through the year.
Consistent with the c.4-5% like-for-like growth guided alongside FY2025 results and with the 5% like-for-like NRI growth delivered in H1 2026.

items.notes: Capex guidance reaffirmed unchanged at the H1 2026 update.

guidance.management_commentary: Management (CEO) framed H1 2026 around four themes: driving operational outperformance in occupancy, footfall and sales; maximising the value of strategic land; increasing scale through accretive acquisitions (notably Manchester Arndale); and raising FY2026 EPRA earnings guidance alongside new medium-term guidance. Management highlighted the highest first-half flagship occupancy in seven years (96%), footfall and like-for-like sales growth ahead of national benchmarks in every region, and continued double-digit positive leasing spreads. On capital structure, management reiterated commitment to an investment-grade credit rating and 'guiderails' of c.35% LTV and 6-8x net debt:EBITDA through the cycle, acknowledging current leverage (8.1x annualised, 39% LTV) sits above the guiderail but expressing confidence in continued deleveraging as acquisitions annualise and further disposals complete (pro forma net debt:EBITDA already down to c.7x reflecting the Dublin Central disposal and Arndale equity funding).

bull_case: Clear, executing growth story rather than a turnaround: FY2025 and H1 2026 delivered consecutive upgrades to earnings guidance (EPRA earnings +5% in FY2025, now guided +27% in FY2026) alongside a newly introduced medium-term 6-8% EPS/DPS CAGR and c.10% total accounting return target — a credible multi-year compounding growth framework following years of balance-sheet repair

Structural 'flight to quality' tailwind: Hammerson's flagship destinations are consistently outperforming national footfall and sales benchmarks (positive in every region in H1 2026, versus flat-to-negative national benchmarks), with four consecutive years of double-digit positive leasing spreads evidencing genuine occupier demand for the best space even as weaker secondary retail struggles

Simplified, fully-owned portfolio: a multi-year programme of buying out joint-venture partners (Bullring & Grand Central, Brent Cross, The Oracle) has converted Hammerson from a complex web of 50/50 JVs into a cleaner, fully consolidated owner-operator, improving transparency, control and capture of full economics from its best assets

Improving credit profile and capital-markets access: Fitch upgrade to A- and Moody's positive outlook (October 2025), plus two oversubscribed bond issues and two oversubscribed/well-supported equity placings in 2025-26, demonstrate strengthening access to capital that supports continued accretive acquisitions (Manchester Arndale) without balance-sheet stress

Embedded, de-risked growth optionality: £291m of strategic land (residential, PBSA, mixed-use) sitting within or adjacent to existing flagships offers low-capital-intensity upside (e.g., The Drum, Ironworks residential, Cabot Gate) without requiring large new land acquisitions
bear_case: Leverage has risen well above the company's own 'through the cycle' guiderails: annualised net debt:EBITDA of 8.1x (reported basis, 9.5x unannualised at FY2025) versus a stated 6-8x guiderail, and LTV of 39% versus a c.35% guiderail, following a run of debt- and equity-funded acquisitions — a classic late-cycle re-leveraging pattern for a REIT only a few years removed from a crisis-driven rights issue

Repeated equity issuance creates a dilution treadmill: two ~10% equity placings in roughly 12 months (August 2025 for Bullring/Grand Central, July/August 2026 for Manchester Arndale) mean per-share growth metrics must continually outrun share-count growth for shareholders to see compounding value, and further acquisitions would likely require further placings

UK-concentrated, pure-play physical retail exposure with no diversification left: having fully exited Value Retail (2024) and VIA Outlets (2020), Hammerson carries no outlet-sector or non-retail (office/logistics/residential-at-scale) diversification to cushion a reversal in physical retail demand, and remains heavily exposed to UK consumer spending, interest rates and planning/business-rates policy

Macroeconomic and geopolitical risk is the company's own sole 'High' residual risk rating — persistent inflation, 'higher for longer' UK rates, weak GDP growth and tariff/trade-war risk are explicitly flagged as largely outside management's control, and a renewed downturn would pressure footfall, occupier sales, rents and valuations simultaneously

Refinancing treadmill continues: significant near-term debt maturities (£609m in 2027, RCFs extended to 2029) mean the Group remains perpetually reliant on open capital markets; the FY2025 Viability Statement itself states 'significant refinancing is required' over the viability period, and interest-cover covenant headroom (75% stress tolerance, 62% in the modelled stress case) is comfortable but not vast

Valuation/NTA has been essentially flat for a year (EPRA NTA per share £3.94 at both FY2025 and H1 2026) despite strong reported earnings growth, suggesting much of the 'growth' is being funded by new capital (debt and equity) rather than organic value creation, and that per-share NAV upside has yet to materialize despite the operational outperformance narrative
